patient.name: Graham Whitfield
patient.setting: GP surgery, then upper GI cancer clinic
patient.complaint: Food sticking behind the lower sternum for 3 months, with weight loss

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with progressive dysphagia (solids then liquids) and weight loss in an older smoker or long-term reflux sufferer; the type and site (adenocarcinoma lower third, SCC middle third) are tested as follow-ups.

points: Graham, 67, says bread and meat **stick behind his lower sternum**.
Started 3 months ago; now even porridge is hard.
Trousers loose: **8 kg lost** without trying.

steps.lead: Graham has the core picture: **progressive dysphagia** for solids, now creeping towards softer food, plus **unexplained weight loss**.

visual.title: Graham's swallowing and weight
visual.caption: Dysphagia worsening month by month while weight falls: a tumour narrowing the lumen, not a motility problem.

steps.q: Dysphagia to solids first, now softer food, with weight loss. What is the leading concern?
steps.r: **Progressive** solids-then-liquids dysphagia with weight loss in an older patient is **oesophageal cancer** until proven otherwise. Achalasia classically affects solids and liquids from the start.

steps.lead: Long-standing reflux, obesity and smoking point to **adenocarcinoma** of the **lower third**, near the gastro-oesophageal junction.

points: Graham also mentions mild **odynophagia** and occasional regurgitation.
Looks pale; no palpable neck nodes.

steps.lead: Graham's voice is normal. A **hoarse voice** would suggest an upper-third tumour (or nodes) involving the **recurrent laryngeal nerve**.

steps.text: Age **55 or over** with weight loss plus dysphagia, or **any age with dysphagia**, means a **2-week wait** referral for urgent endoscopy.

steps.lead: If Graham is diagnosed late, expect **cachexia**, lymphadenopathy, metastases, malnutrition and **aspiration pneumonia** from regurgitated food.

steps.text: Do not label progressive dysphagia with weight loss as 'just reflux' and start a PPI. Dysphagia is an **alarm feature**: refer urgently.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial (or diagnostic) investigation?': the answer is urgent upper GI endoscopy (OGD) with biopsy; CT chest-abdomen-pelvis and EUS are for staging once the diagnosis is made.

steps.q: Graham's GP suspects cancer. What is the first-line investigation?
o: Urgent upper GI endoscopy with biopsy
steps.r: **OGD with biopsy** is first-line and gold standard: it sees the lesion and gives tissue. CT stages; manometry is for motility disorders.

steps.lead: Graham goes on the **2-week wait** pathway via direct access for **upper GI endoscopy with biopsy**.

visual.title: Days from GP referral to endoscopy
visual.label: Graham day 9
visual.caption: Suspected upper GI cancer must be seen within 2 weeks.

steps.title: Bloods on referral
steps.text: **Iron deficiency anaemia** from chronic tumour bleeding and low albumin from poor intake.

points: OGD: an ulcerated, **stricturing mass** at 36 cm, just above the GOJ.

steps.title: Staging once the diagnosis is made
nodes: CT chest, abdomen, pelvis: metastases and distant nodes
EUS: depth of wall invasion and local nodes
MDT decides curative or palliative route
steps.caption: Tissue first, then stage.

steps.lead: Graham's CT shows **no distant metastases**; **EUS** shows the tumour through the muscle wall with local nodes: locally advanced.
After any resection, Graham will have a **follow-up CT at 6 months** after discharge to look for recurrence.
Graham's journey follows the **2-week wait** upper GI cancer pathway and **6-month** post-resection surveillance CT.

steps.text: A barium swallow can show a stricture but **cannot give tissue**. In the exam, suspected oesophageal cancer means **OGD with biopsy**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?' where stage decides: neoadjuvant chemo(radio)therapy then oesophagectomy for locally advanced resectable disease, and endoscopic stenting for palliation of unresectable dysphagia.

points: The **upper GI MDT** reviews Graham's scans.
Locally advanced, no metastases, fit enough for surgery.
Plan: shrink the tumour first, then operate.

steps.lead: Graham's tumour is **locally advanced**, so he starts **neoadjuvant chemotherapy** (or chemoradiotherapy) to downstage it before surgery.
If it downstages, Graham has the definitive treatment: **oesophagectomy**.

steps.title: Treatment by stage
nodes: Locally advanced → neoadjuvant chemo(radio)therapy, then oesophagectomy
Palliation: endoscopic stent or radiotherapy for dysphagia
steps.caption: Curative intent needs resectable disease and a fit patient.

steps.q: If Graham's CT had shown liver metastases and he could not swallow saliva, what would help most?
steps.r: Metastatic disease is **unresectable**: palliate dysphagia with an **endoscopic stent** (or radiotherapy). Surgery would not cure.

steps.lead: For a patient like Graham with metastases, the aim is swallowing and comfort: **stent** or **radiotherapy**.

points: Day 3 after oesophagectomy: Graham spikes a fever.
New cough with green sputum; crackles at the right base.

visual.title: Chest X-ray, day 3 post-op
visual.caption: Right lower zone consolidation: postoperative (often aspiration) pneumonia.

steps.lead: **Postoperative pneumonia** is the complication to watch after oesophagectomy; complete inability to swallow needs urgent assessment for **obstruction**.

steps.text: Oesophagectomy is major thoracoabdominal surgery: chest physiotherapy, early mobilisation and nutrition support (often a feeding jejunostomy) reduce complications.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: which pathological process Barrett's represents (metaplasia), which cancer it predisposes to (adenocarcinoma), and why dysphagia progresses or why neoadjuvant therapy is given.

steps.lead: Years of acid and bile reflux turned Graham's lower oesophageal squamous lining into **columnar (Barrett's)** epithelium, which then progressed to cancer.

steps.q: Graham's biopsy showed columnar mucosa with intestinal features above the GOJ. Which process is this?
steps.r: Replacement of one mature cell type (squamous) by another (columnar) is **metaplasia**. Dysplasia is disordered growth with cellular atypia.

steps.lead: SCC is different: **tobacco and alcohol** act **synergistically** on the native squamous lining, usually in the **middle third**.
Graham's tumour grew **circumferentially**, narrowing the lumen bit by bit: first solids stuck, then softer foods.
Graham needed CT and EUS because oesophageal lymph drains **extensively in many directions**, so nodes can be involved early and far away.
Graham's neoadjuvant therapy shrank the tumour and treated **micrometastases**, giving a better chance of an **R0** (clear-margin) resection.

visual.title: Graham's tumour on neoadjuvant therapy
visual.caption: Downstaging before surgery makes a complete R0 resection more likely.

mcq.q: Which is the most common type of oesophageal cancer in the UK?
mcq.r: **Adenocarcinoma** is more common, arising in the lower third near the GOJ.

mcq.q: Where does oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma typically arise?
mcq.r: SCC is typically **middle third**; adenocarcinoma is lower third.

mcq.q: Which symptom suggests recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement?
mcq.r: A **hoarse voice** points to an upper-third tumour or nodes affecting the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

mcq.q: What pattern of dysphagia is typical of oesophageal cancer?
mcq.r: **Progressive** dysphagia from solids to liquids reflects gradual luminal narrowing.

mcq.q: What is the gold-standard investigation for suspected oesophageal cancer?
Which test assesses the depth of mural invasion?
mcq.r: **EUS** shows depth of wall invasion and local nodes.

mcq.q: What is the usual approach to locally advanced resectable oesophageal cancer?
Which is a palliative option for dysphagia from unresectable disease?
Which premalignant condition predisposes to oesophageal adenocarcinoma?
mcq.r: **Barrett's** (columnar metaplasia) leads via dysplasia to adenocarcinoma.

mcq.q: Barrett's oesophagus is an example of which process?
mcq.r: Squamous replaced by columnar epithelium is **metaplasia**.

prompts.q: What are the two main types of oesophageal cancer, where does each arise and what causes each?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: site and risk factors tell you the type.

points.p: Adenocarcinoma: more common, lower third near the GOJ
Adenocarcinoma risk: GORD, Barrett's, tobacco, diet

points.why: Upper and middle third tumours are usually SCC.

points.p: SCC risk: tobacco, alcohol, achalasia; usually normal BMI
points.why: Achalasia is a classic SCC risk factor in SBAs.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: progressive dysphagia plus weight loss is the vignette.

points.why: Achalasia gives solids and liquids together from the start.
Weight loss plus dysphagia is a 2-week-wait trigger.
See next prompt: recurrent laryngeal nerve.

prompts.q: What does a hoarse voice suggest in oesophageal cancer, and why?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: anatomy question dressed up as a symptom.

points.why: The nerve supplies most intrinsic laryngeal muscles.

prompts.q: What complications does oesophageal cancer cause?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: think late disease and aspiration.

points.why: Extensive lymphatic drainage means early spread.

prompts.q: What is the first-line and gold-standard investigation for suspected oesophageal cancer, and how fast?

points.p: Urgent, within 2 weeks (2-week wait, direct access)
points.why: NICE suspected upper GI cancer pathway.

prompts.q: How is oesophageal cancer staged, and how is it followed up after resection?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: CT for distant spread, EUS for depth.

points.why: Looks for metastases and distant nodes.

points.p: Endoscopic ultrasound for depth of mural invasion
Follow-up CT 6 months after discharge post-resection

prompts.q: How is oesophageal cancer treated, from curative to palliative?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: stage and fitness decide the route.

points.p: Locally advanced: neoadjuvant chemotherapy or chemoradiotherapy

points.why: The only curative option for most.

points.p: Unresectable: palliative endoscopic stent or radiotherapy

prompts.q: What emergencies and postoperative complications must you watch for?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: cannot swallow, or chest sepsis after surgery.

points.p: Complete dysphagia: urgent assessment for obstruction
points.why: Can't swallow saliva means urgent review.
The commonest serious complication after oesophagectomy.

prompts.q: Explain the metaplasia-dysplasia-carcinoma sequence and how SCC differs.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the process at each step.

points.p: Chronic acid/bile reflux causes squamous-to-columnar metaplasia (Barrett's)
points.why: Metaplasia is reversible; dysplasia is the precancer.

points.p: SCC: direct carcinogenic injury; tobacco and alcohol synergistic
points.why: Combined risk is greater than the sum.

prompts.q: Why does dysphagia progress, why is staging extensive and why give neoadjuvant therapy?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: each 'why' has one key phrase.

points.p: Gradual luminal narrowing as tumour grows circumferentially
Lymphatic drainage extensive and multidirectional; early distant nodal spread
Neoadjuvant shrinks tumour, treats micrometastases, improves R0 resection

glossary.adenocarcinoma: Cancer of glandular (columnar) epithelium; in the oesophagus it arises in the lower third from Barrett's.
glossary.squamous cell carcinoma: Cancer of the native squamous lining of the oesophagus, usually in the middle third.
glossary.GOJ: Gastro-oesophageal junction, where the oesophagus meets the stomach.
glossary.GORD: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease: acid and bile flowing back into the oesophagus.
glossary.Barrett's: Columnar metaplasia of the lower oesophagus caused by chronic reflux; premalignant for adenocarcinoma.
glossary.Barrett's oesophagus: Replacement of lower oesophageal squamous epithelium by columnar epithelium with intestinal features.
glossary.metaplasia: Reversible replacement of one mature cell type by another.
glossary.dysplasia: Disordered growth with cellular atypia; a precancerous step.
glossary.achalasia: Failure of the lower oesophageal sphincter to relax with loss of peristalsis; a risk factor for SCC.
glossary.regurgitation: Undigested food coming back up without nausea or retching.
glossary.cachexia: Severe wasting of muscle and fat from chronic illness such as cancer.
glossary.recurrent laryngeal nerve: Vagus branch supplying most laryngeal muscles; damage causes a hoarse voice.
glossary.hoarseness: A rough, breathy voice; here from recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement.
glossary.OGD: Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy: camera examination of the oesophagus, stomach and duodenum.
glossary.endoscopy: Looking inside the body with a flexible camera; allows biopsy.
glossary.biopsy: Taking a tissue sample for histology.
glossary.EUS: Endoscopic ultrasound: an ultrasound probe on an endoscope to measure depth of wall invasion.
glossary.mural invasion: How deep the tumour has grown into the oesophageal wall.
glossary.2-week wait: NHS urgent suspected cancer referral: seen or tested within two weeks.
glossary.staging: Working out how far a cancer has spread to plan treatment.
glossary.neoadjuvant: Treatment given before surgery to shrink a tumour.
glossary.oesophagectomy: Surgical removal of part or all of the oesophagus.
glossary.R0: Complete resection with microscopically clear margins.
glossary.micrometastases: Tiny deposits of cancer spread too small to see on scans.
glossary.endoscopic stent: A metal mesh tube placed across a tumour to keep the oesophagus open.
glossary.MDT: Multidisciplinary team meeting that agrees cancer treatment.
glossary.aspiration pneumonia: Lung infection from inhaling food, fluid or stomach contents.
glossary.downstage: Reduce a tumour's stage, usually with neoadjuvant therapy.
glossary.Plummer-Vinson syndrome: Iron deficiency anaemia with a post-cricoid web causing dysphagia.
glossary.manometry: Pressure measurement of oesophageal muscle contraction, used for motility disorders like achalasia.
glossary.barium swallow: X-ray after swallowing contrast to outline the oesophagus; shows strictures but gives no tissue.

technique.stem: A 70 year old man has a 4 month history of difficulty swallowing. Initially meat stuck behind his sternum; now he struggles with soup. He has lost 9 kg. He has had heartburn for 20 years and has a BMI of 31. He is an ex-smoker.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about dysphagia: decide benign or malignant, then which type.
**Progressive** solids-to-liquids dysphagia plus weight loss means cancer. Long reflux and obesity point to adenocarcinoma.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Lower-third cancer from reflux and Barrett's: **oesophageal adenocarcinoma**.

elim: Achalasia gives solids and liquids together from the start, usually in younger patients.
A peptic stricture follows reflux but does not cause marked weight loss.
SCC fits alcohol, smoking, normal BMI and middle third; reflux and obesity favour adenocarcinoma.
A pharyngeal pouch gives high dysphagia, halitosis and gurgling.

steps.x: **C. Oesophageal adenocarcinoma.** Rule: reflux + obesity + progressive dysphagia = adenocarcinoma.

technique.stem: A 63 year old woman has a 6 week history of food sticking when she swallows and 5 kg of weight loss. Examination is unremarkable. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

steps.x: Initial investigation: the first test that gives a diagnosis.
Dysphagia, weight loss and microcytic anaemia: suspected upper GI cancer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **2-week wait upper GI endoscopy** with biopsy.

elim: Barium swallow shows a stricture but gives no tissue.
CT is for staging after the diagnosis.
EUS stages depth of invasion; it is not first-line.
Manometry is for motility disorders such as achalasia.

steps.x: **E. Urgent upper GI endoscopy.** Dysphagia is an alarm feature at any age.

technique.stem: A 74 year old man has metastatic oesophageal adenocarcinoma with liver deposits. He can no longer swallow solids or liquids and is drooling saliva. He wants to be able to eat and drink at home. His pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management of his dysphagia?

steps.x: Management of dysphagia in known cancer: curative or palliative?

clues: can no longer swallow solids or liquids
wants to be able to eat and drink
steps.x: Metastases mean unresectable; the goal is swallowing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Palliative **endoscopic stent** across the tumour.

elim: Heller myotomy treats achalasia.
Neoadjuvant therapy precedes curative surgery, which is not possible.
Oesophagectomy is not offered with distant metastases.
A gastrostomy feeds but does not let him eat and drink or clear saliva.

steps.x: **A. Endoscopic stent.** Unresectable dysphagia: stent or radiotherapy.

technique.stem: A 58 year old man with long-standing reflux has an OGD. Biopsy of the distal oesophagus shows columnar epithelium with goblet cells replacing the normal stratified squamous epithelium. There is no cellular atypia.
technique.q: Which pathological process does this represent?

steps.x: A pathology-process question: name the change.

clues: replacing the normal stratified squamous epithelium
steps.x: One mature cell type replaced by another, without atypia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Metaplasia**: Barrett's oesophagus.

elim: Anaplasia is loss of differentiation in malignancy.
Dysplasia needs cellular atypia; none is present.
Hyperplasia is more cells of the same type.
Hypertrophy is bigger cells, not a different type.

steps.x: **E. Metaplasia.** Barrett's is the first step to adenocarcinoma.

practice.stem: A 66 year old woman has a 5 month history of difficulty swallowing food and 6 kg of weight loss. Over the past month liquids have also become difficult. She has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 45 years and drinks 40 units of alcohol a week. Her BMI is 21. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Progressive dysphagia with weight loss in a heavy smoker and drinker with normal BMI is oesophageal SCC. Adenocarcinoma fits reflux and obesity.

steps.x: Diagnosis: cancer or not, then which type.
Progressive dysphagia, weight loss, **tobacco plus alcohol**, normal BMI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oesophageal SCC**.

elim: Achalasia: solids and liquids from the start, no weight-loss pattern like this.
Bronchial cancer rarely presents with dysphagia alone.
Adenocarcinoma links to reflux and obesity, not given here.
Plummer-Vinson: iron deficiency with a web, usually women, not this risk profile.

steps.x: **D. SCC.** Smoking + alcohol + normal BMI = SCC.

practice.stem: A 71 year old man has had heartburn for 25 years. He now has a 3 month history of food sticking at the lower end of his sternum and has lost 7 kg. His BMI was 33 last year. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 86 bpm and BP 142/88 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Long-term reflux, obesity, progressive dysphagia, weight loss and iron deficiency anaemia point to lower-third adenocarcinoma. A peptic stricture does not cause this weight loss or anaemia.

steps.x: Diagnosis of dysphagia.

clues: food sticking at the lower end of his sternum
steps.x: Reflux, obesity, low dysphagia, weight loss, microcytic anaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oesophageal adenocarcinoma** of the lower third.

elim: Achalasia is not linked to reflux or anaemia.
Spasm gives intermittent chest pain and dysphagia, not weight loss.
Candidiasis needs immunosuppression and causes odynophagia.
A peptic stricture is benign: no anaemia or major weight loss.

steps.x: **C. Adenocarcinoma.**

practice.stem: A 62 year old man with known oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma has a 3 week history of a weak, breathy voice. He has no sore throat or cough. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his voice change?
o: Vagal trunk involvement below the diaphragm
practice.e: Hoarseness in oesophageal cancer suggests upper-third tumour or nodal involvement of the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm.

steps.x: Cause of a symptom: think anatomy.
Hoarseness without infection in oesophageal cancer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Recurrent laryngeal nerve** invasion.

elim: Candidiasis causes sore throat and plaques.
Phrenic nerve palsy raises the hemidiaphragm, not the voice.
Reflux laryngitis causes sore throat and throat clearing.
Vagal trunks below the diaphragm do not supply the larynx.

steps.x: **C. Recurrent laryngeal nerve.** Hoarse voice = upper third or nodes.

practice.stem: A 68 year old woman has a 4 month history of progressive dysphagia and 10 kg of weight loss. She has smoked for 50 years. On examination she is thin and there is a hard, fixed lymph node in the left supraclavicular fossa. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Progressive dysphagia, cachexia and a hard supraclavicular node mean advanced oesophageal cancer with nodal spread. Thyroid cancer gives a neck lump, not progressive dysphagia with cachexia in a smoker.

steps.x: Diagnosis; note the extra examination finding.
Classic cancer story plus a hard node: **late disease** with lymphadenopathy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Metastatic oesophageal cancer**.

elim: Achalasia does not cause hard nodes or cachexia.
Pharyngeal pouch: high dysphagia, gurgling, halitosis.
Thyroid cancer gives a thyroid lump that moves on swallowing.
TB nodes come with fever and night sweats, often matted.

steps.x: **B. Metastatic oesophageal cancer.** Late disease: cachexia and lymphadenopathy.

practice.stem: A 69 year old man has known oesophageal cancer causing dysphagia and frequent regurgitation of food. He develops a fever and a productive cough. There are coarse crackles at the right lung base. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Regurgitation from an obstructing oesophageal tumour causes aspiration pneumonia, classically right lower lobe. Metastases do not cause fever and focal consolidation.

steps.x: A complication of the cancer: which one fits the picture?

clues: coarse crackles at the right lung base
steps.x: Regurgitation plus right basal consolidation and fever.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Aspiration pneumonia**.

elim: Metastases appear as nodules and do not cause acute fever.
An effusion gives stony dullness and a meniscus, not consolidation.
PE gives pleuritic pain and hypoxia, usually with a clear X-ray.
Fistula with mediastinitis is rarer and causes coughing on every swallow and chest pain.

steps.x: **A. Aspiration pneumonia.** Right lower lobe: the right main bronchus is more vertical.

practice.stem: A 55 year old man with long-standing reflux had an OGD 3 years ago showing Barrett's oesophagus. He did not attend surveillance. He now has a 2 month history of food sticking and 5 kg of weight loss. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 134/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Barrett's oesophagus progresses through dysplasia to adenocarcinoma. SCC arises from native squamous epithelium with tobacco and alcohol.

steps.x: Diagnosis with a known premalignant condition.
Barrett's plus new dysphagia and weight loss.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Adenocarcinoma** via the metaplasia-dysplasia-carcinoma sequence.

elim: Achalasia is a motility disorder unrelated to Barrett's.
Eosinophilic oesophagitis affects young atopic men without weight loss.
SCC is not the Barrett's cancer.
A Schatzki ring gives intermittent bolus obstruction, no weight loss.

steps.x: **C. Adenocarcinoma.** Barrett's = adenocarcinoma.

practice.stem: A 60 year old man has a 2 month history of progressive dysphagia to solids and 6 kg of weight loss. He has smoked for 40 years. Examination is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: Suspected oesophageal cancer is diagnosed by urgent OGD with biopsy. CT and PET-CT are for staging.

steps.x: Diagnostic investigation: the one that gives a definite answer.
Alarm features and iron deficiency: suspected oesophageal cancer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **OGD with biopsy** within 2 weeks.

elim: Barium shows a stricture but no histology.
CT stages but does not give tissue.
Manometry is for achalasia and motility.
PET-CT looks for occult metastases at staging.

steps.x: **E. OGD with biopsy.** Tissue is the diagnosis.

practice.stem: A 64 year old woman has biopsy-proven adenocarcinoma of the lower oesophagus. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no distant metastases. The MDT needs to know how deeply the tumour has invaded the oesophageal wall.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Repeat upper GI endoscopy with biopsy
practice.e: EUS shows depth of mural invasion and local nodes. A repeat OGD sees only the mucosal surface.

steps.x: A staging question: depth of wall invasion.

clues: how deeply the tumour has invaded
steps.x: Diagnosis made, distant spread excluded: now local T stage.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Endoscopic ultrasound**.

elim: Barium shows the lumen, not wall layers.
Bronchoscopy checks airway invasion in upper-third tumours.
MRI is not the standard for oesophageal wall depth.
Repeat OGD sees only the surface.

steps.x: **C. EUS.** CT for distance, EUS for depth.

practice.stem: A 61 year old man has adenocarcinoma of the lower oesophagus. Staging CT shows no metastases. Endoscopic ultrasound shows invasion through the muscle wall with local lymph nodes. He is fit and active. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Proton pump inhibitor and surveillance endoscopy
practice.e: Locally advanced resectable disease in a fit patient: neoadjuvant chemo(radio)therapy to downstage, then oesophagectomy. Surgery alone is for early disease.

steps.x: Management: curative or palliative, and in what order?

clues: invasion through the muscle wall with local lymph nodes
steps.x: **Locally advanced**, resectable, fit.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Neoadjuvant** therapy, then **oesophagectomy**.

elim: A stent is palliative.
Surgery alone is for early disease; this needs downstaging.
Palliative radiotherapy is for unresectable disease.
PPI and surveillance is for Barrett's, not cancer.

steps.x: **B. Neoadjuvant then oesophagectomy.**

practice.stem: An 82 year old woman with frailty has squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus with lung metastases. She can only manage sips of fluid and wants to eat soft food. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Unresectable metastatic disease with dysphagia: palliative endoscopic stent. Neoadjuvant therapy is only given before planned curative surgery.

steps.x: Management of dysphagia in advanced cancer.
Metastatic and frail: palliate dysphagia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Endoscopic stent**.

elim: Heller myotomy is for achalasia.
Neoadjuvant therapy precedes curative surgery.
Not curable and she is frail.
Balloon dilatation is for achalasia; a stent holds a malignant stricture open.

steps.x: **A. Endoscopic stent.**

practice.stem: A 66 year old man had an oesophagectomy 3 days ago. He now has a fever, a productive cough and reduced breath sounds at the right base. His temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 114 bpm, BP 120/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Oxygen, sputum and blood cultures and IV antibiotics
practice.e: Postoperative pneumonia is the key complication after oesophagectomy: give oxygen, take cultures and start IV antibiotics. CTPA is for suspected PE without focal chest signs and sepsis.

steps.x: Initial management of a postoperative complication.

clues: reduced breath sounds at the right base
steps.x: Fever, sputum, focal chest signs, raised inflammatory markers: **postoperative pneumonia**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oxygen, cultures, IV antibiotics**.

elim: PE is less likely with productive cough and focal signs.
A stent is palliative for dysphagia.
He is septic and hypoxic: not for oral antibiotics and discharge.
Nothing suggests a surgical leak needing theatre.

steps.x: **D. Oxygen, cultures and IV antibiotics.**

practice.stem: A 57 year old man with locally advanced oesophageal adenocarcinoma is told he will have chemotherapy before his oesophagectomy. He asks why he cannot just have the operation now.
practice.q: Which is the main reason for giving chemotherapy before surgery?
o: To allow the oesophagus to heal before anastomosis
To shrink the tumour and treat micrometastases for complete resection
To stimulate the immune response to the tumour
practice.e: Neoadjuvant therapy shrinks the tumour and treats micrometastatic disease, improving the chance of an R0 resection.

steps.x: A 'why' question about neoadjuvant therapy.
Locally advanced disease: big tumour and possible occult spread.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Downstage the tumour and kill **micrometastases** for an **R0** resection.

elim: Chemotherapy delays healing; it does not help it.
Chemotherapy does not prevent pneumonia.
Chemotherapy does not treat reflux.
This is cytotoxic, not immunotherapy.

steps.x: **D. Shrink tumour and treat micrometastases.**
